newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end higher on early dive in stocks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end higher on early dive in stocks.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries rose early in the session and never looked back, ending moderately higher on Monday, as the market was boosted by early deterioration in stock prices and a stronger dollar.
"The stock market was dictating a lot of flows," said one head trader at a European-based primary dealership. "There was a lot of asset allocation (from stocks to bonds) going on."
Stock prices, which plunged on Friday, spent much of Monday's session weaker, with the Dow Jones industrial average down as much as 83 points in the afternoon.
But stocks staged a furious late-day rally, with the Dow ending 80 points higher. Yet the rise in stocks barely made a dent in Treasury prices.
Late Monday, the 30-year bond was at 98-3/32, up 11/32 from Friday. It had been up as much as a half-point early in the afternoon. The bond's yield fell to 6.52 percent from 6.55 percent.
A strengthening dollar helped the long end of the market. Last week, a falling dollar hurt Treasuries.
The dollar was at 117.95 yen and 1.8340 marks in late day trading, up from 117.90 yen and 1.8200 marks at the open.
"People are looking for direction," said one trader. "Watch stocks and watch the dollar and that will tell you what is going on."
Indeed, Monday's econonic calandar was bare, with only so-called minor data due out this week.

At 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Tuesday, housing starts for June will be released, followed at 0900 EDT by the BTM-Schroders weekly chain store sales report, July import/export prices at 1000 EDT and the Redbook weekly retail sales report at 1440 EDT. The data were not expected to have much market impact.
Also, the Federal Reserve's policy setting committee meets but no change in rates were forecast.
Therefore, stocks, the dollar and technical factors will dominate activity on Tuesday, market participants said.
On Monday, even as the market was reacting to the gyrations in the stock market, technicals played a part in the continuation of the bond market's rally.

The September contract, for instance, broke through its 114-4/32 resistance level, rising as high as 114-12/32 before retreating to 114-3/32 at the close. The market was said to be eyeing 114-15/32, a 50 percent retracement from recent lows.
Treasury prices opened higher on Monday, on buying from European central banks and retail accounts.
Activity was very light, with volume at around $55 billion. One trader said that if not for the early stock to bond re-allocation, most of the Street would have been on the golf courses.
Thomas Estes, head trader at SBC Warburg, said the stock trade was overstated. He said that the market would have been "considerably higher" if there had been a concerted outflow from stocks.
Others argued that the early strong performance of the short end was helped by the stock trade, much like on Friday when a "flight to quality" was reported as the Dow industrials fell 3.1 percent.
Three-month bills closed down one basis point to yield 5.12 percent. Six-month bills were up one basis point at 5.15 percent and year bills were unchanged at 5.21 percent.
The 10-year issue was up 7/32 at 99-12/32 to yield 6.21 percent. The five-year was 2/32 higher at 99-25/32 to yield 6.05 percent and the two-year was unchanged at 100-3/32 to yield 5.82 percent.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
